# Discussion

Returning to the hypotheses, the results provide partial support for
**H1**: the plant signal predicts valence above chance (p = 0.005) and,
more weakly, the crossed emotion label (p = 0.015), whereas arousal
does not reach conventional significance (p = 0.055). H1 is therefore
supported for valence and for the crossed emotion label, but not for
arousal.

The secondary analysis addresses the most plausible alternative
explanation for that result. **H2** is rejected, tested on valence as the
dimension for which H1 holds. Both
branches of the confounding pathway are in fact present — CO~2~
correlates with valence ($\rho$ = 0.308, p \< 0.0001) and, in the raw
analysis, with most plant features — so the alternative explanation was
not implausible a priori. The decisive condition nonetheless fails: the
plant–valence association remains essentially unchanged once CO~2~ is
controlled for, so it is not an artifact of a shared dependence on
ambient CO~2~.

## Interpretation of our Findings

For each target variable, two feature representations were compared:
raw, in which plant-derived features enter the model on their original
absolute scale, and session-normalized, in which each feature is expressed as
a robust z-score relative to the median and spread of its respective
recording session. This distinction addresses a key property of the
sensing setup: the DC level of the plant voltage drifts between sessions
due to factors such as ambient temperature and room-level CO~2~
baseline. These factors are unrelated to emotional state but can shift
the absolute voltage range across sessions.

Since each session corresponds to exactly one participant, a classifier
trained on raw voltage levels could implicitly associate specific
voltage ranges with specific participants, rather than learning a
genuine relationship between signal dynamics and emotional state. This
constitutes a form of session-level leakage that may inflate apparent
performance without reflecting true predictive signal. Session
normalization mitigates this issue by removing session-identity
information and re-expressing each feature relative to its
session-specific center and spread prior to training.

The results support this interpretation. For valence, session
normalization increased the average macro-F1 score across all three
classifiers by 0.031, with the largest gain observed for Random Forest
(+0.068). For arousal, the average macro-F1 score improved by 0.035. In
both cases, the best-performing models used session-normalized features,
and the features those models ranked highest are either level-invariant by
construction or expressed relative to the session's own baseline — which
is what the leakage argument above predicts.

Emotion classification is the only case in which this pattern did not
hold: Random Forest performed slightly better on raw features (0.21)
than on session-normalized features (0.19). However, this difference is
small relative to the overall variation across all six model-feature
combinations (macro-F1 0.17 to 0.21) and is therefore more
likely attributable to performance variability among similarly
performing models than to a failure of session normalization for this
target variable.

Arousal remained the weakest target variable overall, with performance
close to chance and the best result narrowly missing statistical
significance (p = 0.055). This is consistent with a known limitation of
the arousal axis, which relies exclusively on RMSSD and mean heart rate:
the work of Choi et al. [@choi2017] suggests these markers are reliable
indicators of emotional state only for unpleasant, highly arousing stimuli, not for
neutral or pleasant ones. Since the video stimulus combines strongly
negative segments with comparatively mild or neutral ones, only part of
the recorded material may fall within the range where HRV is expected to
track arousal at all, independently of any limitation in the plant
signal itself.

The correlation analysis complements these findings. While CO~2~ showed
substantial correlations with plant features in the raw analysis, these
associations decreased markedly after removing between-session variance.
This suggests that most of the observed plant-CO~2~ coupling reflects
slow session-level drift rather than within-session physiological
interaction. Importantly, the plant-valence relationship remained stable
under CO~2~ control at both levels, indicating that this association is
not an artifact of shared environmental influences.

## Comparison with Previous Studies

The present study directly addresses the two central limitations that
Gloor [@gloor2025] explicitly identified: the lack of a standardized elicitation
protocol and the single-subject design. By employing a fixed, ten-minute
video stimulus instead of post-hoc labeling of unconstrained behaviour,
and by recording 15 participants with grouped cross-validation to
prevent participant-level leakage, the present study constitutes a
multi-participant replication of this experimental paradigm with a
controlled emotion-elicitation protocol.

The shift from a binary "happy"/"sad" classification to a dimensional
valence-arousal framework [@russell1980] further extends this
replication methodologically: it allows for a more fine-grained analysis
than Gloor's binary scheme permitted, and reveals that plant signals are
informative for valence but not for arousal — a distinction that could
not have been captured within a binary classification framework in the
first place.

Both studies validate their findings via permutation testing, supporting
the conclusion that the reported results in either case are unlikely to
be driven by data leakage. However, a direct comparison of raw accuracy
values (72.8-73.8% in Gloor [@gloor2025] versus 36-43% across the six
valence combinations in the present study) is
complicated by differences in class distribution and evaluation metrics:
Gloor [@gloor2025] reports accuracy figures from an imbalanced (60/40)
classification task without a macro-F1 or comparable metric. Because
accuracy alone may overestimate performance when classifiers favor the
majority class, it is difficult to assess to what extent the accuracy
reported by Gloor [@gloor2025] reflects genuinely balanced discriminative
performance rather than class-imbalance effects. This limits the
comparability of the two accuracy figures beyond a coarse indication
that both are above chance level.
